title: Nvidia reassures robotics startups it backs after Jensen Huang's exit
excerpt: After Jensen Huang's exit, Nvidia contacted robotics startups to reassure them of its support amid questions about its investment strategy.
content_html:

Nvidia tells robotics startups they have its support as questions swirl about its investment strategy

By Rya Jetha

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-17T19:03:17.399Z

Nvidia is reaching out to robotics startups with a message after Jensen Huang's sudden departure: The chipmaker still has their backs.

Since Huang's resignation, the company and its venture capital arm, NVentures, have contacted at least three robotics startups they back to reassure them of its support, Business Insider has learned. The calls began last Thursday, shortly after Huang's resignation, with startups assured that business would continue as usual.

The outreach comes amid uncertainty about Nvidia's broader investment strategy under interim CEO Colette Kress, who is not expected to pursue deals as quickly as Huang and has sometimes pushed back on investments he championed.

Nvidia declined to comment on the calls.

Under Huang, Nvidia became a major backer of robotics and "physical AI," the term he popularized for AI that can act in the real world. At the company's conferences, he often appeared onstage flanked by humanoid robots. Huang described robotics as the technology industry's "first opportunity to address a $50 trillion industry that has largely been void of technology until now."

That enthusiasm translated into investments in more than 35 robotics and physical AI companies, according to PitchBook data. Of these, 29 have disclosed funding rounds totaling nearly $11 billion. Nvidia's portfolio includes humanoid makers Figure AI and Neura Robotics, robot foundation model developer Skild AI, self-driving software company Wayve, and autonomous trucking startup Waabi.

The robotics investments are part of a broader push that made Nvidia a financial backer of much of the AI ecosystem. At the end of July, it held $48 billion in stakes across 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Deepu Talla, an Nvidia robotics vice president who worked on some of the company’s investments, told Business Insider that Nvidia intends to "continue to aggressively cultivate the ecosystem.”

Nvidia's robotics products brought in $11 billion in the first half of this year, 30% more than in all of 2025, Talla said. Some of that revenue comes from companies Nvidia has invested in.

The company's robotics strategy has two parts: developing the simulation tools, software, and chips that power robots, and investing in startups building them. The investments can turn startups into customers while giving Nvidia a stake in their success.

"If you look at any cap table of a company that is compute-heavy, Nvidia is probably there, because they knew much of that money was going to flow back to them," one investor whose firm has backed multiple startups alongside Nvidia, told Business Insider.
